title: The Poet's Three Copies
synopsis: A young poet copied his book of poems by hand, three times.
The friend's copy is gone. He comes at sunrise.
goal: Find the copy Yun Dong-ju made for his friend, and give it to his friend at dawn.

notes: Played under the glass (InspectScene) on Yun's desk: the thick book with a red spine is the one his words describe; the folded note under it is the label, its last word worn.

The blue drop is Miri's sign: she brings water to the rooms (M1 letter), and she does not write her name so the office man cannot know who wrote it (final talk). The bottle of blue ink is the near miss: the drop on the card is drawn, not spilled.

Measured 2026-11-06 on the grid sheet of dorm_room.webp (picture.measuredOn): the blue ink bottle on the left, the two string-tied copies, the thick red-spined book with the folded note under its corner, the desk lamp; no two areas overlap.

discovery.detail: Miri took it. Her card may tell where.

notes: Played as two records compared (RecordsScene): Yun's list for his friend's copy and Miri's card, which copies it line by line. They agree on the copy (2 of 3), the friend (Jeong Byeong-uk) and the poems (18 + 1 opening poem), and disagree only on the string: WHITE on the list, BLACK AND WHITE on the card.

The reasoning is the player's: the list agrees with what Yun said in M1 (the friend's copy had a white string), so the card's line is the untrue one, and untrue on purpose: with the card's last words (keys of these colours) it reads black and white keys. The piano is never named in M2; M3 shows it.

Redesign 2026-11-07 (docs/SEOUL_CASE11_STORY_REVIEW.md, option A): replaces the Hangeul stroke riddle (syllable_compose, 피아노안), which had no ground in Yun Dong-ju's story. Chosen by hand for that reason: the puzzle teaches the copies' facts (h2, h3) and gives M3 its numbers.

Measured 2026-11-07 on c11_copy_list.webp and c11_drop_card.webp (picture.measuredOn): each blank sheet's four corners by brightness edges; the list a tall sheet (flat 340x454), the card a folded sheet (flat 340x443, rows kept off its two creases; its water drop at about flat 321,422, right of the note's column).

Both papers and their words are made up (dossier fiction); the copies, the friend's name and the poems' count are facts (h2, h3). The words are the app's text over blank sheets: no writing in any picture.

clueInputs.note: Miri's card under the dictionary: a card that copies Yun's list.

evidence.description: Miri's small wooden box, hidden inside the college piano, with a number lock.

notes: Miri's lock (made up) takes two numbers from Yun's list (M2's evidence, shown to Miri in the talk before): copy 2 of 3, so three copies (h3); 18 poems and 1 opening poem, so 19 (h2). Side by side, copies first: 319. Every number is on this case's own list.

The talk before the lock: Miri tells why she took the copy and why she signs with a water drop; she asks for the paper in Yun's own hand. Her own card (e1) copies the same numbers but is not in Yun's hand; the box (e3) is no paper.

intro: Schools must teach in Japanese now.
Yonhi College, Seoul. You visit poet Yun Dong-ju.
He could not print his book. So he copied it by hand, three times.
The friend's copy is gone. He comes at sunrise.
play.caseSummary: Miri brings water to the college rooms. A man from the office was checking the rooms. So Miri hid Yun Dong-ju's copy in her box, inside the college piano. Her card, signed with a water drop, pointed to keys of black and white. At dawn, the numbers on Yun's list opened the box. Yun gave the copy to his friend. Yun wrote his poems in Korean when Korean was pushed out of the schools. In 1948 they became a book.

notes: Season 5 Case 11 (PART 10, 2026-11-06). Yun Dong-ju is real; everything he says and does in the case is made up. Miri, the office man checking rooms, Miri's box and its lock and the piano are made up.

Real outcome kept: three handwritten copies (teacher Lee Yang-ha, friend Jeong Byeong-uk, himself), the friend's copy hidden by his family and published in 1948; the case ends on the checked fact that Yun wrote his poems in Korean when Korean was pushed out of the schools.
No line of his poems is quoted or translated; only the book's title is given in English.
Yonhi College was, as far as known, a men's college in 1941: Miri helps at the college (she brings water to the rooms) and is never called a Yonhi student (not source-checked).

Redesign PART 4 (2026-11-09, docs/SEOUL_CASE02_12_REDESIGN_PLAN.md §C3 Case 11): M3 is PIANO (the two meanings of keys, and the card's colours); the 319 lock moved to the final, after Miri's talk; KOREAN final removed.
